text_fidelity_a:
Samsung 32GB up to 48MB/s EVO Class 10 Micro SDHC Card with Adapter (MB-MP32DA/AM) Deciding to catch up on my product reviews – I was ELATED this particular Micro sD card is no longer available. I know that’s a bit mean-spirited, but I can’t help it. I was out the money for the item because it was past Amazon’s 30-day return window.

I purchased one in October of 2015 for my Samsung GS4, and only two (2) months later – I needed a brand new one. Why? It failed. No warning, nothing. Just a failure.

And this wouldn’t be the first failure either.

The sD card I bought in December failed as well, but I’ll give it up for it – It went OVER three (3) years before failing. It failed April 3, 2019. I remember that because of the event it failed during. I would’ve expected the failure when I transferred the sD card from the S4 to the S8 in May 2018, but the card still worked.

There were no signs of pending failure or issues. The night before (4/2), it worked and I was able to retrieve some photos off of it.

My mother and I went to Knott’s Berry Farm for the Boysenberry Festival. And, any photos take before we left – GONE. No error messages – just gone. I didn’t know until I got home.

What photos I have were the return photos from the drive home. I had briefly
glanced at the card data (on my phone) at about 2pm, but after that (without being dropped, banged, over-heated) the card failed. I know some will ask why I didn’t back them up – I was in transit, driving on the freeway, so it wasn’t feasible.

All I know is that my photos were gone.

So, I had to purchase another sD card for my phone. This time I chose the GREEN Evo Select one. And, from April 2019 to the date of this review, it’s been pretty solid. Though I’m not taking any chances. I store photos to my S8 as well as the sD card.

Since it isn’t available, I won’t bother with saying I don’t recommend it. I certainly won’t buy it again if it does become available again.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung 32GB up to 48MB/s EVO Class 10 Micro SDHC Card with Adapter (MB-MP32DA/AM)

What it DOES do is light upgradually, letting you know it's time to get up.

I highly recommend this, even though it seems expensive. The FIRST time you get up at 6am without being dragged behind a 1989 GMC conversion van with Guatemala license plates you'll know this thing just paid for itself.

text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic SC-BTT195 Energy Star 5.1-Channel 1000-Watt Full HD 3D Blu-Ray Home Theater System with Tall Boy Speakers Good sound for the money and does what I expected. Skip to the summation if you are looking for reasons not to purchase.

Might be a better choice especially if you own a Panasonic TV as the set up is designed for a Panasonic product line. I had to use their support call service a few times and as most companies today, some are very good and can understand and help, but most will read a prewritten script and hope they hit on the problem you are experiencing. Cons: Had to go buy after market speaker wires due to the lack of length that comes with the system and splice the wires to place the rear speakers. Also had to buy an audio connector to allow the system to produce TV sound. This really ticked me off and Panasonic should really step up and correct these issues. The system also needs to modernize and add another HDMI connection ( and the cable ...really? ) to allow for a cleaner install. Another con is the system will not produce sound while watching the Internet based VUDU movie channel. Panasonic wanted me to buy another movie and call them to "try" some fixes while the movie played! It does work with my cable provided paid movie service. The system would also not work with my top of the line wireless router and had to buy a cable and run wires to their system. One must also buy another adapter ( Dingle) to receive wireless signals that may or may not work or a connecting cable. Check to see see the distance from your router to the system and if it is physically possible to fish the wire to the sound system from the router before you buy the cable.

Summation: "You get what you pay for". If you can splice wires and figure out how to add cables to make TV audio work and the internet work then it's ok. You will need to spend more money on items that should be included from Panasonic and it is best to own a newer Panasonic TV for easier installation. Panasonic kind of ruined what should be a great experience by cutting corners to save money on wire and connections. Panasonic should provide more installation on information "needs" as part of their product description if they aren't not going to provide long enough speaker wire, HDMI connectors and inputs,or audio cables,or internet Dingle or cable.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic SC-BTT195 Energy Star 5.1-Channel 1000-Watt Full HD 3D Blu-Ray Home Theater System with Tall Boy Speakers

text_fidelity_a:
VIZIO M70-C3 70-Inch Class Ultra HD Full-Array LED Smart TV Based on Vizio M65 - C1 4K Ultra Smart TV with 240 Htz.

As a few others I have experienced the picture going black on the set after a few hours of operation followed by in my case a loud snapping noise. I lowered my rating based only on this phenomenon . Amazon as always stood by the sale and made everything more than right . IF it had not been for the going to black concern , my rating would have been five stars .Contacting Vizio resulted in being asked to perform a bunch of resets and chanting magic incantations ( joke ) . That was considered when raring the product too. When not going black , the picture is amazing ! Sporting events in particular pop off the screen and the detail seen is incredible. First time ever my cable box has registered 1080P . I can't speak to the 4K aspect as I have not attempted to watch anything in that range . The black range is as crisp as I have ever seen on any set. Setup is very easy and uncomplicated. The remote includes a key pad on the back to make entering information and searching easier. Again , would be a five if not for the picture going black issue.

Con: The speakers are tiny and are facing the rear . Not sure why they choose to go the cheap route and skimp on the sound. By no stretch am I an audiophile but one does notice the lack of depth to the sound and the volume level needs to be up to hear dialog clearly. A sound bar is almost a requirement and I did see that some retailers are packaging one with their Vizio TV'S to,address this concern.
The remote has a quick access buttons for Amazon , Netflix and of all things IHeart Radio. They must have got a kick back from I Heart . The quick connect feature loose a plus for choosing I Heart. Hulu or the like would have been a better choice .

I would not be afraid to buy this set. I would strongly suggest that the purchase be supported by a vendor you trust and will support the sale after the fact. Some of these are through a third party and directly through Amazon . I always select the direct Amazon route because of the support after the sale. I needed it in this instance and as always was not disappointed by Amazon customer service.
text_fidelity_b: VIZIO M70-C3 70-Inch Class Ultra HD Full-Array LED Smart TV

Logitech HD Laptop Webcam C615 with Fold-and-Go Design, 360-Degree Swivel, 1080p Camera I was able to compare this directly to the Logitech C525. They both have the same "fold and go" design, but I was surprised that the C615 is a bit heavier, and I think a millimeter or two thicker. It's well worth it, because the optics are better, and not just better because the resolution is higher - the quality is simply better.

The tripod mount is a nice addition over the C525, adding versitility in positioning. I suppose this would also help you set it up as a hidden camera, or just keep a pile of dirty laundry out of the view mounting on your laptop might otherwise provide.

As others have mentioned, there is a USB extender, which is nice. However, I would much rather have seen a long (or even a very short) cable provided with a microUSB connection to the actual device, allowing the device to become truly portable, rather than having a nice foldable, portable device with a cumbersome cord permanently attached. The user could then use the same cable they charge their smartphone with. Thankfully, the cord is placed in such a way that allows for full 360 degree rotation.

Note that although you can record 1080 videos with this device, you can only chat in 720 - another consideration if you just want this for Skype or another chat program.

Overall, this is the most appealing webcam on the market to me. The most important thing is that it can be tossed in a bag or pocket with other electronics without having to worry about the lens getting scratched.

text_fidelity_a:
G.G.Martinsen Crystal-faceted 8 GB Mini Usb Port Multi-lingual Selection 1.8 LCD Mp3/Mp4, Video Player, Music Player, Media Player, Video player, Audio player With a Slot for a micro SD card--Black I have been offered three different G.G. Martinsen players free or at a discount in exchange for my honest review. I like this one better than the first one I got ([[ASIN:B0173CW2CQ an 8GB player]]), but because I went into detail in that review on the different functions (that this one also has), I've copied the functional descriptions from that review below. I'll just compare this one to the pink one in terms of what's different.

I like the black color of this, the ability to put it on a keychain or lanyard, and how small it is, but I don't like the way it all handles nearly as much as I do the [[ASIN:B0168C6MB4 16 GB player]] that I will review separately. The controls and settings are just awfully fiddly and not terribly intuitive. That you can add up to 16GB extra memory via an SDHC card (for a total of 24GB) is a boon, and that's the only thing I like better about this player than the 16GB one; the latter does not have an expansion slot. It's a useful thing if using a player like this when exercising if you can swap out different kinds of music for different types of activity—what works for running or walking will be different than what you'd use for swimming or dancing, for example. But still, these players all hold a decent amount of music natively, and you can also copy a ton of files to it if you're using it to double as a flash drive.

Here's the original functional review for this type of player:

The first thing I tried was the FM radio, because I was really doubtful it was going to work very well in my bedroom, but I was able to pull in NPR and the voices were crystal-clear. The earphones that come with this look really cheap, but they sound pretty good. As with any earphones, they don't cancel surrounding sounds, which makes them perfect for going out for a nice brisk walk. I actually prefer earphones to earbuds because earbuds never fit my ears right. These are like the original Apple earphones, and they stay in my smaller ears really well. I think it's a nice touch that these earphones are included with the player because you can use them in situations where you don't want your really good headphones to get lose or ruined. The device has the following menus, accessible by pressing the Menu button, then the right play button to cycle through them.

SETUP: It's very fiddly trying to set these settings. It takes a lot of trial and error to get it all to work. These are the settings: Clock, LCD Set (not sure what this is), Language (came set to English), Power Off (I can't figure out how to get into these settings to set the times to zero so the player doesn't shut off too soon, so this is why I'm knocking it back to three stars), an Online Mode, Firmware Upgrades, Memory Info.

MUSIC: Navigating through music is straightforward cycling through folders and files. I set up a Walking Songs folder and also dragged my whole Collective Soul Folder with Subfolders to the device, and I was able to navigate between the folders before playing. Selecting specific songs is more difficult. I've never learned how to create playlist files (I know, I know), so I can't say if those will work. There is a funky little equalizer animation on the screen when you play a song.

VIDEO: There's actually a nice music video included on the device, and it will play over and over if you don't stop it. I can see that this might make it possible to put together a loop of items to keep a child entertained on a trip, but it might also have utility for studying, memory work, a flash-card-like experience, or the like.

RECORDER: What it is. Records in .wav format at 32kbps. Great for quick reminders or embarrassing your friends.

VOICE: Used to play back recordings.

FM RADIO: Works great on the stations I've tried, without an antenna of any kind. I may have to start listening to more radio while I'm working.

PHOTO: A simple photo viewer, so you can keep all the pictures of your pets or kids that you'd normally have in your wallet to inflict on the people you meet. I'm just learning about QR codes (scanned my first one on my phone the other day), but I would think you could generate QR codes to carry on this device as well. The device does not recognize .png or .eps files, but it reads .jpgs fine, even larger ones (which do take a bit more time to load).

EBOOK: This is for reading simple .txt files. Don't think you can put anything proprietary like Kindle ebooks on it; it didn't read the .mobi file I copied onto it, or the .epub, or the .pdf. But who'd want to read a whole big book on such a tiny screen anyway? Use the EBOOK capability to take grocery lists or short paragraphs of instructions with you.

GAMES: I almost forgot the games. I'm not a game player. There are a handful of games that I haven't bothered to look at.

This player is not a super-fancy high-end piece of electronics, but it's a lot of bang for the buck and also something you wouldn't die over if you happened to lose it. Of course, you can always use it instead of a flash drive to take files with you different places for subsequent transfer. So it's a lot of functionality in one small package.
text_fidelity_b: G.G.Martinsen Crystal-faceted 8 GB Mini Usb Port Multi-lingual Selection 1.8 LCD Mp3/Mp4, Video Player, Music Player, Media Player, Video player, Audio player With a Slot for a micro SD card--Black

text_fidelity_a:
Kensington Orbit® Fusion™ Wireless Trackball (K72363WW), Black I used a Logitech M570, a thumb trackball, for years until I started gaming again and needed a gaming mouse. Now I’m done with gaming for a while and have been searching for a trackball to reduce strain.

The Kensington Orbit Fusion Wireless Trackball is the first Kensington trackball I’ve tried.

I hate the scroll ring. I think this is either a feature you love or hate, and well, I just don’t like it. Using the scroll ring is uncomfortable for me; I keep going back to my laptop trackpad instead of using it. It’s too easy to move the trackball while using the scroll ring, and I couldn’t decide which finger was most comfortable for using it. I spent a lot of time fiddling with the scrolling speed in the KensingtonWorks program, but content doesn’t move smoothly on my screen -- it jumps.

The mouse is too big for my hand. I usually wear a size small in women’s winter and nitrile gloves, to give an idea of the size. My fingers have to stretch too much to reach the left and right click buttons at the same time. My hand rises off the mouse when I use the scroll ring.

I know some of this is muscle memory, but my wrist and hand actually hurt after using the trackball for more than a few minutes.

I do like that KensingtonWorks can be used on Windows or Mac. I’ve tried a lot of high end gaming mice that I can’t always customize on my Mac. KensingtonWorks lets you modify the pointer, scroll ring, and customize the buttons. You can also back up your settings to Google Drive or Microsoft OneDrive, and set options for specific programs. Kensington also included a USB-A to USB-C adapter.
text_fidelity_b: Kensington Orbit® Fusion™ Wireless Trackball (K72363WW), Black

Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous Generation - 7th) - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity - Includes Special Offers When I first purchased the Kindle Paperwhite, I did so because I had an older Kindle (keyboard version) and some of the letters on the keyboard ceased working. I did a lot of research before I traded in my old Kindle. I really liked the reviews on the new Paperwhite version so decided to purchase it. I had to replace my first Paperwhite because the refresh screen turned every screen black. Customer service was excellent and when it was determined that we could not reset the kindle I received a new one. I waited until now to write this review (it was purchased earlier this year) because there were many differences and wanted to make sure that the review gave the Kindle what I felt it deserved.

First, I must say that I love many of the features of the Paperwhite version: it is small enough to fit in my purse, the font is easy on the eyes, the back-light is great in any light, the dictionary feature works well and I love the fact it has a vocabulary builder. It is very easy to download books and to access my library; it is also easy to locate different pages in the book.

However, the reason I rated the PaperWhite a 3 is because of the page turning (I have had no further problems with the refresh). Sometimes with light touch it will not turn the page or it will skip 3 or 4 pages and you have to back up to your last read page, which I find very annoying. I had more control with my older Kindle as it had a button on the side that allowed you to control the page turns and wish that the Paper White had the same feature. Other than this, the Paper White has a lot of great features but I am very disappointed with the page turn function.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous Generation - 7th) - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity - Includes Special Offers

I have a smartphone, but it's getting harder for me to read on it. I have an iPad Air, but even that can be a little big on a cramped plane ride.

Plus, I sold my other seven inch tablets (a Galaxy and a MeMo), and I miss them. They're the perfect size for reading. This tablet is so much nicer than what I would have been willing to deal with for fifty bucks. However, there are a couple of issues that keep this from being a five star device, even at this price.

The first is that using an sd card to hold content is no easier than it is with the older tech media players I have spent a fair amount of time trying to figure out. If you can download it to your computer, you can put it on the card and then load the card into the Kindle, but the Kindle doesn't treat the card like a drive that you can save to. A firmware update could fix this.

The second is the weight. I'm actually not sure how I feel about this one. It's definitely heavier than I expected. But it feels solid. So, maybe I like it?

Everything else is great for what I am using it for. Reading books. Very light web browsing. Playing with my FireTV. Buying music to play on the Echo. In other words, it's a great tool for accessing the Amazonverse. As a regular tablet? Good for the price.

Conference call after conference call after conference call. I’m working from home with a house full of kids out of school and dogs I’m not usually working around.

1. Noise Cancelling. It helps to drown out the house noises which helps me focus.

2. Comfortable. Oh my gosh. No joke. I have two piercings in each ear and for the most part I’ve been avoiding headphones because they hurt unless I take my earrings out. I can wear these all days and they don’t hurt.

3. Holy Battery Life, Batman! My AirPods need charging several times a day. My other Bluetooth headsets also have poor battery life. I can, quite literally, go a day or two without charging these. At the very least, I can go through my full day of calls without needing to charge.

4. Sound quality is excellent. Volume is excellent. Both audio and mic.

The one downside, as far as I’m counting, is that my phone for some reason doesn’t default to the headphones when I answer. I have to answer, it shows as the headphones for audio, then it goes back to my phone audio and I have to re-select the headphones. It’s such a small thing compared to all the amazing things these headphones do.

I’ve been recommending them to everyone, from my elderly father to my coworkers. I replaced my AirPods with a new set of AirPods right before I ordered these. I thought you would pry my AirPods from my cold, dead hands. I was wrong, I was so, so wrong. I wear these listening to audiobooks while doing the dishes, and the noise cancelling amazingness drowns our the sound of water and lets my hear the story. I drown out my Rottweiler defending the house from the mailman so I can hear what the CEO is saying in my meeting. It drowns out four children in their Zoom classes all working in the room with me. Some of the LED's that ruin my night vision are small but raised, so I size up on those to cover the entire protruding bulb.

There are two sheets of this translucent sticker material. This first sheet is pre-cut shapes of varying sizes and the second sheet is meant to be cut to size as you see fit. I've used that for the large lit On/Off switches on surge protectors! You can dim any light or display with it! These sheets have upgraded my home, for real. They look nice, are stackable, and I can walk through my dark, non-blinding house at night again without being assaulted by nerve-damaging bright and seriously overused LED's. Now I just need to get these on the headlights of every car and truck in the world.......

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Harmony 950 Touch IR Remote Control - Discontinued by Manufacturer So far this is my initial view of this remote just having downloaded the software and set up the initial action. Logitech, you guys need to have your heads examined. It's a REMOTE. I should not need a computer in the first place to set up a REMOTE. To add insult to this injury, they claim since I have macOS Catalina that their 32-bit software will not work. Ah, hello McFly? 32-bit apps?? Seriously? The 20th century called, they want their tech back. We've been using 64 bit for at least a decade. It is 2020 now. You know... Unbelievable. If you can't write software, fold it all up and go home. You don't deserve our money.

First mistake by Logitech. Ultimately, there IS a 64-bit app. So why do you still have a message on your web site saying we'll need an update? Here's a tip for you guys. YOU CAN JUST SUPPLY the 64-bit app right there on that screen. You could easily say for Catalina and above, click here, else get the older, lamer, 32-bit version. I have to click on a link, which seems to tell me you don't have it, which goes in a bit of a circle, before ultimately telling me that you do in fact have it.

Next, the 950 has this super stiff cover for the Micro USB connector, also technology from the cretaceous period. I think we found one of these cables in the mouth of Coleophysis bauri remains from 250 million years ago. I wasn't sure if I was breaking the thing or pulling off a cap. You software asks if I have a hub for my remote? I bought it, I didn't build it. I have whatever came in the box. Is it a hub, a charging cradle, a spacecraft, an anti-gravity device, a floatation device? I don't know. All I know is I put the device in that thing and your software doesn't detect it. So I proceed to PRY off that cap, hoping it was a cap, and it is. It would be nice if the TINY manual said so.

Before I actually try to use this thing, one more note for you brainiacs at Logitech. It would super if you made the remote with a flat back. I'll give you a guess why I say this. When you make a rounded back, us, meaning your customers, can't leave the remote on a flat surface and press the buttons without it wobbling all over the place. It pretty much becomes a two-handed operation. As luck would have it, I have two hands. But you never know. It would be super if I can just put it on a flat surface and USE it while it sits on the hard surface of, say a coffee table or nightstand.

At this stage, I'd give zero stars if possible. Hopefully the remote can redeem itself in practice. But all this nonsense to get using it in the first place is almost a deal killer. In fact, I'd bet that alone is a deal killer for many.

More to follow.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Harmony 950 Touch IR Remote Control - Discontinued by Manufacturer

and while it doesn't technically matter and is certainly not reflected in my rating, i just don't like the looks of the thing. it looks cold and evil. i was going to say "like Darth Vader sitting on my desk", but i never thought Darth Vader looked this...unsettling.

that's just my psychology though, and, as i say, of no actual consequence.

four stars because it does perform marginally better than the router it replaced, and the web interface is both fairly easy to use and gives much more control than AirPort Utility does.

what i wish i knew, and have looked for online to no avail, is how to optimize the myriad settings to be sure i'm getting the best performance this unit has to offer. i spent $400.00 on a router expecting great things and i'd like to get them if at all possible, and i don't know how, or whether i am. and a downside of having such extensive control over the router's settings (while not knowing how to optimize them) is that there are surely a lot more ways to run it at less than its full capability than there are to get the best out of it. can anybody point me to a good step-by-step guide on how to maximize this router's performance?

I bought this after reading a ton of threads and reviews on the JMC583 chipset and how it worked pretty well with the latest firmware update. However, after getting this external drive kit and setting it up with a SamSung 970 EVO NVME drive and updating to the latest JMC firmware, it worked okay for Windows workloads but it had serious problems with Linux on a Raspberry Pi 4B. tons of UAS reset errors. Even tried it with the UAS bypass workaround and still it had resets.

Additionally, the drive gets really hot with use. hot to the touch and almost worrisome. I know this may be somewhat normal for NVME drive enclosures but it definitely feels above my personal safety threshold.

I'm going to try a different drive enclosure next with the RTL9210 chipset as I've read more favorable reviews on that.

text_fidelity_a:
Blink Whole Home Bundle | Video Doorbell System, Outdoor camera, and Mini camera | HD video, motion detection, Works with Alexa "Set up in minutes"?? Not really. There are no actual detailed instructions included. I tried scanning the QR code that was provided in the little pamphlet, and that was not helpful. This ended up being extremely frustrating to set up. I could take a wild guess that I was supposed put the lithium batteries in the back of the camera. I would not have known that the little QR code inside the camera where the batteries go was something that I had to scan to set up the camera. Anyway, without going into detail, if Amazon provided some simple, basic instructions with photos that show step by step, it would save the customer a ton of fumbling around. Then it might have been an easy set up. I had to call for support, and by the time I got a support person on the phone I was pretty irritated. The reason I decided to buy this camera is the "two-year battery life." Note: these are not rechargeable batteries. We'll see how long the batteries last. Prior to this, I got a Eufy Solocam, also wireless (and much, much easier to set up), and it had rechargeable batteries advertised to last 4 months, but they lasted 4 weeks. A feature that is missing with the Blink camera, that I liked on the Eufy camera, is the AI feature to recognize humans. Without the AI feature, the Blink is recording non-human motion, such as animals and vehicles.

Update: The description advertises customized zones for motion detection. The camera takes a photo what it sees, and in motion settings, you gray out areas that you do not want the camera to detect motion. It does NOT work. I tried resetting it several times, and the camera recorded and sent me an alert of motion detected that was squarely in the grayed out area. Without this feature actually working, and without the AI feature to detect humans, the camera is recording every motion in the entire viewable area, ignoring the areas that I grayed out. I am returning this camera.
text_fidelity_b: Blink Whole Home Bundle | Video Doorbell System, Outdoor camera, and Mini camera | HD video, motion detection, Works with Alexa

Trezor Model T - Advanced Crypto Hardware Wallet with LCD Touchscreen, Secure Bitcoin & Over 1450 Coins for Maximum Security I've used a lot of Trezor Ones over the years so I'm really comfortable with the Trezor name and their uses as a hardware wallet. Their reputation is great and the open source nature of their product has set the bar for a lot of competition.

The model T is a marked improvement over the Trezor One. The model T has support for Shamir Secret Sharing which allows you to easily split your recovery seed into multiple parts. The color screen and size also allow for more things to be displayed and verified on the Trezor T. This makes inputs on the device a lot easier than it's predecessor. i.e. when you are inputting or checking a recovery seed or pin, it is a tedious process on the One and very easy to do on the Model T.

The only downside to the Model T is the price. It seems expensive and the build quality could be better. Something about the plastic casing and shape makes it seem cheap. The small screen in comparison to other products make it also seem cheap. For example, Cobo Vault Pro costs approx $150 and has a much larger touch screen and better overall build construction; look and feel wise. At $165 for the model T, the build quality seems very different.

Would I buy another Model T? If the price point were around $100 I would definitely buy many more model Ts. As it is, with a price point of $165, I have opted to buy other competing hardware wallets, Cobo Vault, ColdCard, etc. as I don't think the price to value is quite right for the Model T.

Like all those articles say, when these companies war, we all lose. And now Apple, we don't trust you. Finance that reputation recovery, right?

Pros:
It is somewhat faster loading a movie than the 3rd gen.
The addition of apps is neat
The voice recognition of the remote is shockingly great considering the failure of Apple's Siri
Higher definition

text_fidelity_a:
Antennas Direct ClearStream 1MAX HDTV Antenna UHF VHF, Multi-Directional, 40+ Mile Range, UHD 4K, NEXTGEN TV – w/Adjustable Mounting Hardware (Black) Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

So far so good!
text_fidelity_b: Antennas Direct ClearStream 1MAX HDTV Antenna UHF VHF, Multi-Directional, 40+ Mile Range, UHD 4K, NEXTGEN TV – w/Adjustable Mounting Hardware (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
A-TGTGA Fitness Tracker with Heart Rate Monitor, Activity Tracker Smart Watches, 1.71" Full Touch Smartwatch with IP68 Waterproof, Message Notification Sleep Monitor, for Android iOS What I like about this watch:
- one full charge lasts several days
- good way to track your BPM, Blood pressure, calories burn, steps taken
- could make phone calls with the watch
- if you take the watch off for whatever reason (like to shower) it doesn't keep taking your BMP or blood pressure so you don't have to worry about your data getting messed up/ inaccurate.
- comfortable silicone band which has a lot of holes to adjust to your size wrist, I have a very small wrist and use the second to last hole
- good size screen, not too large and not too small
- you could set alarms (through the app) also features a stop watch and timer
- receive and check notifications for several apps plus text messages
- has a find phone feature if you misplace your phone
- you could add music to your phone (which I have not done, and not sure if I'm going to do)
- waterproof
- Compatible with my Samsung smartphone, and easy to set up

dislike:
- only 4 different dial face designs to choose from
- speaker is towards the bottom so sound could be blocked by your arm depending on your position
- sleep tracker is not very accurate (while I'm laying in bed reading, watching a movie, or on my phone it thinks I am sleeping, and there is no way to edit the hours manually)
- no power button (to turn on or off)
- you cannot name or write notes with the alarms, there are only icons to label
- does not stay connected to my phone in my whole house. If I have my phone on charge in my living room and I'm in my kitchen which is 2 rooms over, I will not get notifications from my phone
- app doesn't not always update, I will have to go to the app and refresh (down swipe) for data to refresh and update
- charger connection is magnetic and a couple times it was bumped while on charge and the charger got knocked off and I didn't know, do it wasnt charging. Plus if the charger breaks for whatever reason I don't have a back up.

Cable Matters DisplayPort to DVI Adapter (DP to DVI Adapter) My desktop computer has a built in graphics card on the motherboard and I added a graphics card for gaming. The graphics card has a DVI, VGA and DisplayPort outputs. I had two monitors hooked up, one to the DVI, and one to the VGA port. I had another monitor (actually a TV) which duplicated screen two using a splitter. But I wanted to use it as a third separate monitor.

I tried several things to make a third monitor work: a DVI to HDMI cable (not an active cable) didn't work - the computer never saw the third monitor. I also tried the built in graphics card on the motherboard, plugging in an HDMI cable to its port and connecting the TV. That didn't work. it seems only one graphics card can be enabled at a time; either the one on the motherboard, or the installed graphics card.

This worked. As soon as I plugged it in, going from the displayport on the graphics card to the HDMI cable, the computer saw & recognized the 3rd monitor. Now I have three separate monitors.
text_fidelity_b: Cable Matters DisplayPort to DVI Adapter (DP to DVI Adapter)

Echo Dot (4th Gen) | Smart speaker with Alexa | Twilight Blue The spherical Echo Dots do not sit well with the various echo holders. If you are thinking of wall mounting this device you'd do better by buying a small platform/shelf to place it on. The indicator light is on the bottom. This gets hid easily by the various Echo Dot wall mounts. Like all Echo Dots, they are great to control smart devices but get very poor marks in understanding the elderly and those slow of speech. As one who is elderly, wears dentures, and hard of hearing, I don't get my words pronounced with distinction. Echo will usually respond with something it found on the web that has zero relation to what I asked of it. My wife is slow of speech and the echo will cut her off and try to process the fragment without waiting for her to complete. I have submitted a request to Amazon about this to have a final key word to denote end of speech but they have not made any changes to the software, nor replied to my comments.
Overall it is a worthwhile device to have. With as many smart devices that we have to simplify our life this has been a Godsend. However, its impatient teen attention span is annoying when trying to issue commands or to have it actually find something on the web...like we asked.

text_fidelity_a:
ASUS VS197D-P 18.5" WXGA 1366x768 VGA Back-lit LED Monitor, Black I'm very pleased with this monitor. I needed to replace my second screen and didn't want to spend a lot, but needed a monitor with 1920x1200 resolution. This seemed like a decent bet. It has exceeded my expectations with regard to performance. The clarity is excellent -- it rivals my primary screen which cost three times as much!

The monitor is very lightweight. It comes with both DVI and VGA cables, which was unexpected. I like that there's no power transformer or wall wart. It has just a regular power cord. Set up is simple (just attached the base and no tools are needed).

Of course, at this price point some features are not present. For example, while the screen can be tilted back and forth a bit, it does not have any up/down adjustment, nor can it be swiveled into portrait mode. There's no USB connectors and no speakers. But for me, none of those were deal breakers. I wanted a good quality monitor that was affordable, and this hit the mark 100%. Plus, it does not scrimp on connections. There's DVI, VGA and HDMI. I'm using DVI at present since the PC I'm using it with is a few years old. But, my next PC will probably have a HDMI connection, making this monitor future-proof (well, as future-proof as any tech product can be).

If you're looking for a basic monitor that does not scrimp on image quality, this should definitely be on your short list. Also, check Amazon Warehouse for used ones. I got mine there (it was probably a customer's return). It looks brand new, and only ran me $127.
text_fidelity_b: ASUS VS197D-P 18.5" WXGA 1366x768 VGA Back-lit LED Monitor, Black

text_fidelity_a:
ACPRO600 Good: Nice, minimal fit for my medium DSLR (canon 70d) with medium zoom lens (18-135) with lens hood on. Not too tight but not too much extra room. Seems to be well made. I like that it has a rain protector hidden in a lower pocket, but it'd be better if the case itself was weatherproof (is it that hard? Case Logic claims theirs is...)

Not so great: Pretty minimal pocket space outside the main compartment. Enough for a battery, a lens brush, memory. Not enough room for a lens blower, or other bulkier accessories. (Certainly no room for another lens, but you wouldn't want that in a holster.)

BAD: Strap. It's too short. I am not a big person (5'6"), and if you use it as a shoulder strap (isn't that how everyone uses it?) the camera will come nowhere near your hip. I have it adjusted to be as long as possible and still had to extend it with a couple of carabiners. That's ridiculous. Some reviews noted a well padded strap. Sort of. It has a sliding shoulder pad which is nicer than many. A little softer.
But it does slide around and I often find it's not on my shoulder after a while (the strap itself is just a basic nylon strap).

Maybe an issue? It'd be nice if the top of the bag was a bit wider. It takes me a little extra time to get the camera out because I have to squeeze my hand between the camera & bag. It's not tight - but just another 1/2" would be nice. That's going to vary with your camera.
Also, the bag doesn't let go when I lift the camera. The lens gets caught on the yellow camera support thingy a little bit, so I have to hold the bag with one hand while I pull the camera with the other. I suppose that's why gunslingers used to have a thong that tied the bottom of the holster to their thigh. That'd work - even if it looks a little silly...
text_fidelity_b: ACPRO600

Creative Aurvana 2 In-Ear Headphones (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I was really impressed with the Aurvana 2. For about a hundred bucks, this is an incredibly versatile set of earphones that can handle most any genre of music very well. They always presented a balanced sound stage, with crispy clean highs and warm smooth bass. My quibbles with the Aurvana 2's are few. The included carry case has a hard plastic molded frame that fits the earphones perfectly and allows you to wrap the cord. The problem is, it limits the ability to pop an iPod shuffle or small adapter or extension cord into the case with the 'phones. I would also like to see a variety of tips included (beyond just small, medium and large sizes of the same design), because I still have a hard time getting mushroom tips to stay in my ears. Some double flanged or foam tips would be appreciated.

If you are looking for an affordable yet dramatic upgrade to the el-cheapo ear buds that came with your iPod, the Creative Labs Aurvana 2 should be on your short list. I can't honestly say that earphones costing three times as much sound three times better - they don't. Of the dozens of earphones I have tested, this is the perfect intersection of price and performance.

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black I really like this GPS sports watch so far. Garmin makes a huge range of sports watches. This vivoactive HR is one of their lower priced GPS watches. It doesn't have the more advanced sports training features or build quality of the more expensive Garmin Fenix and Forerunner watches. However, for this price, you do get GPS and smartwatch features in addition to basic fitness tracking.

I tried the GPS mode on a 3-hour bike ride, running my dedicated bicycle computer at the same time. Distance calculations of the 2 units were less than 1 mile different, which I think is very good for small portable units like this. Current speed was always about the same, though looking at the watch to see your speed while riding is kind of difficult, especially compared to the big display on my handlebar-mounted bike computer. You can mount the watch on your bicycle handlebar, but that would of course disable the heart rate tracking feature of the watch. The wrist-based heart rate monitor is not as accurate as a chest-strap heart rate monitor, with a slower response time that is very apparent during interval training (short bursts of high-intensity effort), but you can connect an ANT+ HR monitor to this watch to improve accuracy.

GPS mode has an advertised battery life of 16 hours, which I think is really terrific for a gadget of this size. My 3 hour bike ride burned about 20% of the battery on the vivo, so 16 hours of GPS time is plausible. Garmin also advertises 8 days of battery life with the GPS turned off, but realistically, who buys a $250 GPS watch and never turns on the GPS? Still, I expect to get in at least a couple of long bike rides or several runs before having to recharge this watch. Recharging is very quick using the USB charging cradle included with the watch. Because battery life is so good, you don't need a spare charger for your office like you might need with the Apple smartwatch.

If you have a (free) Garmin account, you can upload your daily activity to the Garmin server so you can review it on their website afterwards. This is useful for tracking your fitness progress (speed, distance, etc) over time.

The smartwatch features are pretty basic (compared to dedicated smartwatches from Apple or Google), showing phone call caller-ID and copying notifications from your smartphone (via Bluetooth) and displaying them on the watch. If you like checking your notifications quickly and don't want to pull your phone out every time it beeps, getting them on your watch is great. If I'm jogging or in a business meeting or at dinner but am expecting an important message, I can just glance at the watch and quickly ignore it if it isn't important. I have my notifications for high-priority emails, SMS, and a couple of messaging apps synced with my phone. This seems to work mostly flawlessly with my Samsung smartphone. Occasionally, the notifications will stop working but restarting my phone fixes that. I don't know if that is a problem with the phone's base software or with the Garmin app that runs on my phone. The Garmin app that runs on your smartphone lets you pick which app's notifications to show on the watch. I do not know how this works with Apple phones. There are some other smartwatch apps like weather forecasts and calendar, but I'm not sure if scrolling through these on your small watch face is really easier than pulling out your phone to view the app on the larger screen there.

If you're comparing this Garmin watch to an Apple smartwatch, yes Apple has a lot more apps, but Garmin has an 8 day battery life compared to less than 1 day for Apple. Personally, battery life is more valuable to me since there are not yet any killer apps for the Apple watch. Having a dead watch because you forgot to charge it the night before is not fun. Also, the Garmin watch has a built-in GPS, while the Apple watch does not. This means you can record a bike ride or run carrying only the watch, not your phone as well.

Garmin also has basic fitness tracking features like resting heart rate, sleep tracking, intensive exercise tracking, step counting, etc. If you're active enough to want to spend money a GPS sports watch (instead of a cheap fitness band), I don't think the step counting is going to be interesting to you. I bike or run at least 10 hours every week of the year and steps have no interest to me. Resting heart rate is an indicator of your health and fitness and I'm looking forward to tracking that. Intensive exercise tracking may also be useful if you tend to slack off during your exercise. Sleep tracking is reportedly not too accurate on this watch (it can't tell if you're really sleeping or reading a book in bed), but that isn't something that greatly interests me.

On the subjective side, this chunky plastic rectangular watch does look like a fitness tracker rather than a real watch. The much better looking Garmin Fenix looks like something you could wear to the office, but this watch maybe not. At least the vivoactive has a very comfortable wristband that should fit well on a range of wrist sizes.

Again, this is one of Garmin's cheaper GPS watches. I think the features and performance are great for this price point, but if you're involved in hard core training program, you should definitely look at the features of some of Garmin's better GPS watches.

I would have given this watch 5 stars for functionality and value for the price if it was better looking, but Garmin seems to have made it intentionally ugly in try to upsell you on their better looking and more expensive Fenix and Forerunner watches.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Motorola T200TP Talkabout Radio, 3 Pack GMRS walkie-talkies like this have been around for decades. Unfortunately, the technology hasn't really improved in all that time. The specs that are listed in the description are greatly exaggerated. We only get 4-5 hours of moderate use from the rechargeable batteries. Fortunately, you can replace them with fresh AA batteries in the field to extend your usage time. The 20 mile range is really a hoax. Even the most optimal situation when one of us is on top of a hill and the others are visible in the valley below, we've never gotten more than 10 miles. In clear flat situations like across a lake or a farm field, range is a 3-4 miles at best. In a forest or city where there are lots of obstructions, range can be less than 1 mile.

20 years ago, few people had cell phones so these radios were really popular. Not so much anymore. That means you get much less interference on each channel. We find the radios useful for family outings since the kids don't have cell phones and many of the parks we visit have terrible cell phone coverage.

The radios are fairly lightweight (about 6 ounces each including the batteries). The package includes 3 battery packs and 2 chargers. One of the chargers has a splitter so it can charge 2 radios at the same time. You can also use your micro-USB cell phone charger to charge the radios. You can also use your own rechargeable AA batteries with your own charger. Replacing the batteries is kind of a hassle since the belt clip blocks the battery cover, though I suppose that also helps keep the battery cover in place. No carrying cases or storage case is included, through the radios are pretty durable and the shipping box works well for storage.

Note that USA use requires a Federal FCC radio license. The photo here is from the instruction manual. Many (perhaps most) users violate Federal law and use them without license, but who knows what enforcement will be like in the future. Other countries have stricter laws and I have heard about some tourists getting into trouble using radios like this.
text_fidelity_b: Motorola T200TP Talkabout Radio, 3 Pack

This Intel Core i3-based laptop is astonishingly, agonizingly slow. I bought this to replace a 7 year-old MacBook Pro that had served well, but didn't have the horsepower to run the latest version of OS X. This Acer is only marginally faster than the MacBook, and feels slower in may respects. It's glacially sluggish to start-up or restart, and Excel and Word crawl along at speeds reminiscent of 1980s era PCs. Browser speeds - Chrome, IE, and the execrable Edge - all range from stagnant to plodding.

Other, more minor, negatives: the track pad might as well be 50 shades of gray, because it requires an extremely firm touch. The PC case is some form of black plastic that shows every fingerprint and smudge, all of which are impossible to remove.

I'm hoping for a day-after-Thanksgiving miracle deal to replace this cinder block of a PC.

Update 08.16.2017: Acer contacted me after this review was posted (big plus), and opened a case. They called me less than 24 hours after the case was opened (another big plus), but they had my laptop registered to someone else and I had to call them back when I had the laptop in front of me. The person I spoke with had me shutdown the laptop, and use a utility to reset system configurations to the default. When I restarted the computer, the performance had not improved. The support person commented that the laptop only has 4 GB of memory, which apparently makes it unsuited to running Excel. Acer sold the computer with this configuration, and no mention of not being able to run the MS Office suite (or open more than one tab on a browser). He then suggested wiping the computer and resetting it to the original state. I'm not willing to invest any more time in this laptop. Thanks to Acer for contacting me, but this one-star review stands. No more Acer products for me.

text_fidelity_a:
Nuforce NE-700X Titanium Coated In-Ear Headphones - Aqua Silver Update after a couple of months

I still love 'em. Everything I put below still holds true. I rarely touch the EQ, and have been able to return to less processing is good processing listening.

One thing to add is that these are the first earbuds I could lay on my side with my head on the pillow and be comfortable. They have minimal strain relief but so far the cords have been perfect. I'd call tangle factor about medium.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
Original review

So far I've tried
Skull Candy Titan - For me the best bass sound in this bunch. Tight punchy, accentuated but enjoyably so. Good for working out. But I value accurate bass above all. So I just use these for working out now.
Vsonic GR99 - very nice balanced sounding for $20ish dollars
Vsonic VC02 - Great sounding, but not a lot of bass. But what bass that was there was VERY good. My favorite phones in this list. But I kept losing the ear piece because of the removable wires. After the 2nd time I moved onto the VSD1
Vsonic VSD1 - nice sounding, if somewhat dry. It didn't make me get into my music, and I couldn't get them comfortable in my ears
Brainwaves S1 - These were my least favorite, boomy and not very comfortable, heavy thick wires. The only pair of the above I returned.

What they do well - assume anything not here is more than adequate

Presentation - I feel like I'm getting what the engineer was going for in the mix. More musical than any of the above without falling into a 'warm sound'. A nice mix of forgiving and accurate. Brightness right about where it should be.
Sound Stage - Airy, instruments well placed. Center image is not the strongest, but not lacking. Does a nice job of presenting the room acoustics/reverb in the mix.
Drums - Drums are rendered very well, better than any of the the above.
Cymbals - rendered very well, especially high hat. You can tell the cymbals are made of metal, and not just the tik-tik of the drum stick tip
Treble-sibilance - Close to perfect. Nice and bright without getting into hissy/tizzy. Vocal articulation is good.
Very easy to listen to for long periods of time. They are accurate without being piercing or harsh.
Sounded good right out of the box.

Misc sound notes - distorted electric guitar is just right. They respond to EQ very well, (which the Brainwavz did not do). I really notice when something comes into the mix even if it is soft. And louder things like guitar solos, really punch in the way you hear when mixing in the studio.

If I HAD to critique the sound (this is a review) there is a very-very, (did I mention very?) lack of something in the mids. Think chest/throat area of male vocals. But this is in the realm of sound signature, a matter of taste, not a deficiency and in no way lowers my enjoyment of these.

Build - wires are thin and flexible which is what I wanted. Very nice for wearing over the ear. Microphonics close to none whether worn up or down. No hearing foot steps or wire rubbing/bouncing on clothes. Light cord/cinch is great for running.
Shape - Bullet shaped what can I say, they are light and comfortable. I like the ring of rubber around them. It gives a little grip for inserting/removing them.
I LOVE that they have a red strain relief on the right side. No having to get my glasses to see some tiny R or L printed somewhere. Cord is nice and long, which is nice for using on a treadmill or elliptical trainer, or for wearing the cord under your shirt or down in a pocket.

As much as I liked the over all presentation and frequency response I feel I should point out these are not hella flat-accurate phones (like the VC02). If a true hi-fi sound, bright/accurate/revealing, is what you are after I'd look elsewhere (maybe the VC02) Don't get me wrong, since I used to be a sound engineer, and work on electric guitars, and have very accurate/bright/revealing/fatiguing speakers on my desk, I'm very picky about good accurate sound. But that makes these musical, easy to listen to for very long periods of time and poorly recorded and/or lower quality rips won't be hard to listen to.

The title says it all - the best I've tried yet and the first phones that made me stop 'shopping' for my next pair of phones.

Listening setup. Listening has been through an amp and separate dac connected to my computer playing 192kb - 320k - FLAC music, and through my old Droid Charge (I use this because I can enable the onboard DAC) and my Samsung Note II listening to ripped music (192k or better) or Spotify/Pandora at their highest quality settings available in the premium versions.
text_fidelity_b: Nuforce NE-700X Titanium Coated In-Ear Headphones - Aqua Silver

text_fidelity_a: Jaybird Freedom F5 In-Ear Wireless Bluetooth Sports Headphones – Secure Sports Fit – Tough All-Metal Design – Blaze I watched a few YouTube videos to get more info about these headphones. I received white but the black might have been a better choice for me. Lots of ear plugs and wings in various sizes, plus a clip and a devise to shorten the cord if it is still too long for you. I usually have an issue with the skip while wearing wireless but these did not skip so far. To be able to listen to a full song without that blank interruption is great. Some reviewers do have an issue with the extra weight the external battery adds, in addition to making the headphones feel off balance. I do not exercise wearing these, so I have not experienced that issue. I tried pairing these with two different phones, a Samsung Note 4 Edge and a Sony Xperia XA Ultra. The sound was tinny on my Samsung and there was little bass. I downloaded the Jaybird app from the Google Play Store and installed it on my Sony. The sound was better on my Sony but with the app, it was amazing. Being able to select different setups or customize my listening preferences really helped. I tried listening to both music and audio books.  Both sounded great. The biggest drawback of these headphones is that you can only recharge them through attaching the external battery. If I lose the battery, the headphones become useless. Overall, these seem great so far. We will see how they age with wear. Hopefully, the company with offer additional external batteries for purchase.

My new house has limited drops and roughly 3k Sq Ft over 2 floors and have no issues. My WD's have over 160 Mbps indicated on the utility from top to bottom.

Nobody will ever mistake it for a several thousand dollar DSLR, either in price, weight, or picture quality, but the 12x zoom in such a small package was the sweet spot for me. And lets face it, for most of us, being able to get the shot because you have your camera is much more important than the really high quality picture--that you're never going to blow up to room size anyway--that you would have got if only you hadn't left your big, heavy, awkward DSLR at home!

The battery is pretty small, though, so make sure you have two or three, which I have always done anyway (they're small, so it isn't that big a deal). Be careful if you buy an off brand battery: Many of them have LESS capacity. Don't go by the picture, many of them appear to be photoshopped to say 1000mAH, but the specs give you the real value. I picked up the [[ASIN:B004M640YU Wasabi Power Battery for Canon NB-9L and Canon PowerShot SD4500 IS, ELPH 510 HS, ELPH 520 HS, ELPH 530 HS]], and it seems OK so far, but I haven't rigorously tested it. TenmaTec Voice Recorder with Playback,80GB Voice Activated Recorder with DSP Noise Reduction,Dual Microphones, Mp3,Speaker,Password Protect,for Music,Overdubbing,Studio,Dictation,Interview The build quality of this little portable recorder is great. It's metal, not plastic, and has a nice heft and feels durable. It looks great. And audio quality is very good. It comes with a micro SD card already installed and ready to go. It also comes with a set of ear buds, a lavalier microphone which can be used instead of the built-in mics, a cord for line-in recording, and a USB charging cord. No charger is included. And it does not come with a protective pouch or sleeve. But it is boxed nicely.

It records in user-selectable WAV or MP3 formats in various selectable bitrates. It has adjustable gain control and a noise reduction function. One important function for voice recording is the ability to monitor while recording using ear buds or headphones, and this recorder has that capability. The display screen isn't as sharp and clear as it is portrayed in the listing photos, but it is decent.

Now for the minor negatives, for which I dinged a star off the review rating. One is the printing labeling the buttons on the one I received is only a little lighter than the color of the recorder, making them very hard to read. That means you have to memorize the button location and functions or keep the user manual handy for reference. And that leads to the second negative, and that is the print in the user manual is tiny. Really tiny. I looked for a PDF version online and couldn't find one. The manual suggests visiting the brand's web site, but neither the manual nor the box provide a URL. Or even the listing brand name (Tenmatec) for that matter. I wound taking photographs of the manual pages with a tablet so I could enlarge them for easier reading. The other minor negative is that it has no USB-C port, only a micro USB for recharging or connecting to a computer for moving files around.

Other than that it's a good recorder. It has one-button functionality (although there is a slight delay when starting a recording while it starts up). Because of its metal construction and heft it feels good in-hand and looks really good.
text_fidelity_b: TenmaTec Voice Recorder with Playback,80GB Voice Activated Recorder with DSP Noise Reduction,Dual Microphones, Mp3,Speaker,Password Protect,for Music,Overdubbing,Studio,Dictation,Interview

text_fidelity_a:
adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - Night Grey, 2.8 x 5.6 x 7.5 Inches I wear headphones when I work outside, spring through fall. By the end of fall, that year’s pair is pretty nasty from hours of daily use and me sweating in them. Of course I clean them, but it’s impossible to *really* deep clean headphones.

So that’s what drew me to the adidas RPT-01 Sport Headphones: the description advertises “removable, washable knitted ear cushions.” Knit covers I can wash? Hooray!

But there’s no instructions in the box on how to remove the ear covers or the headband. It turns out the cushions aren’t as removable as advertised.The ear cups twist off the headphones (a gentle, counter-clockwise turn), but there’s still an inner plastic rim. I thought I’d be able to wash the knitted cover itself, but nope. And I nearly tore the cover trying to figure out how to remove it, until I found the manual online.

I can’t figure out how to get the headband all the way off. The black plastic lining is removable, allowing the headband to be pushed up. I worry the headband will tear quickly, as the holes that line up with the black plastic lining aren’t reinforced.

text_fidelity_a:
RCA BRC10GR Bathroom Clock Radio (Green) Updated review:

I've become somewhat dependent on the sight of this bright blue radio. Every morning I stumble, groggy-eyed, into my bathroom. Having this clear-sounding radio, blasting my favorite music, is a nice pick-me-up as I shower. But does the design offer me anything more than what I would expect from a typical shower radio?

PROS: It's cleverly designed to mimic the shape of a shampoo. It melds easily into the background. My initial fear was that I would accidentally grab it instead of the real thing, but so far that hasn't happened.

PROS: The sound quality is tinny but quite decent for a shower radio.

PROS: The radio offers a "store" function where you can bookmark your favorite radio stations and get to them fast by using a "recall" button. This is a feature common to most clock radios but I don't spend enough time in the bathroom to use it. I basically stick to one station while showering and can't see myself using the "store" function unless I'm taking a long bath. Still, nice to have that option.

PROS: Great battery life! I used my AA batteries for this and it has been running for months with no problem.

CONS: It's not that easy to see the buttons. They're located on the sides of the device but the positions are not intuitive. I always have to squint a little to see the print above the buttons because the buttons do not stick out.

CONS: "Light up" function. The time display is very clear and easy to read as-is. Since it's not a bedtime clock radio that benefits from having a glow-in-the-dark function, this feature feels extraneous to me. Perhaps it's best for someone who likes to take a bath with candles all around.

CONS: Not space saving. I used to have a shower radio that could be hooked over the showerhead. While the radio is not huge, I still had to move my shampoo and conditioner bottles to make room for it.

Overall it is a decent radio and I have been using it since I got it with no problems.
text_fidelity_b: RCA BRC10GR Bathroom Clock Radio (Green)

Between that, the higher cost, and a few other things, I'm in the market for a different tablet and computer.

In the past, the problem switching back was that, unlike with Apple, things were not quite as user friendly with the interface and you had to really figure things out instead of it being immediately apparent.

Happily, it was different with this tablet. Out of the box, my family and I were able to figure it out quickly and easily, giving us hope in another option.

Quality: Great image on the screen with very high resolution! The feel of the device is also sturdy, aesthetically pleasing, lightweight, and thin.

User-friendly layout, very accessible, good features, and it works seamlessly with Google. I've got google email and YouTube channels, so it's nice to know there's a trade-off for losing some of the other things like seamless transitions between iTunes, my current calendar (not in love with that--I can just as easily switch to google or droid for this)...

All this adds up to the following: Apple can no longer claim to be the clear leader in tablets, phones, and computers. They have stopped innovating far beyond comparable products, and now, for the value and overall performance, the ZenPad is a worthy adversary.

I still have my MacBook Pro computer, but when it comes time to buy a new one, I will be ready to switch knowing items like these are available.
What a great surprise!
text_fidelity_b: ASUS ZenPad 3S 10 9.7" (2048x1536), 4GB RAM, 64GB eMMC, 5MP Front / 8MP Rear Camera, Android 6.0, Tablet, Glacier Silver (Z500M-C1-SL)

If you position the Touchpad correctly the on/off button works fine, and the volume button sort of works (can lower the volume easily but raising it requires a bit more effort).

Original review:
This is probably the most useful accessory I've every used for the iPad. Truly amazing in how it can be folded and unfolded to provide ease of use regardless of how you're using the iPad.

All the options make for a bit of a learning curve, however. I tried to follow the diagrams in the user's guide, but didn't really "get" how to use this until I watched the manufacturer's video. Highly recommend that as a guide to how to get the most out of this stand.

I'm especially pleased with being able to use it as a stand for viewing a movie (the position they call "Popcorn and a Movie" in the manual). Excellent when more than one person want to view the screen.

I can't comment with any degree of certainty as to it's longevity since I've only been using it for a few days, but it seems very sturdy. I'll update the review should that assumption prove faulty.

My big question is whether it will fit the iPad 2. Clearly it will cause problems with the cameras, but it is such a tight fit with the iPad 1 (which is a good thing in a case for security) that I'm hopeful that it will work with the iPad 2 with (perhaps) a bit of padding to make up for the thinner profile. I'll update with my experiences with the iPad 2 later this month once I have one in hand.

But regardless of fitting other models, this is an outstanding accessory for the iPad 1. Highly recommend.

It is easy to operate especially with automatic setting and it takes some great pictures. It is also very reliable. As you have with any other purchase, there are pluses and minuses, and the pluses outweigh the minuses.

PLUSES:

1. Quick and easy to turn on and off
2. The compact size of the camera
3. Good quality video recordings in addition to great still photographic capabilities
4. 14 megapixels resolution.
5. Rechargeable lithium-ion battery and the charger could be plugged directly into an outlet with no cables.
6. The flash feature allows you take pictures simultaneously with and without the flash.
7. The Photobook assist, which allows you to mark the pictures
8. Motion panorama feature for panoramic shots

MINUSES:

1. I did not have any issues with the size but some users may find this a little too small to take pictures effectively. It is just 28.1mm thick and 97mm wide at the body

text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic LUMIX DC-ZS70S, 20.3 Megapixel, 4K Digital Camera, Touch Enabled 3-inch 180 Degree Flip-front Display, 30X LEICA DC VARIO-ELMAR Lens, WiFi (Silver) Oct. 2020: If you're photographing foliage with a lot of stems & leaf edges, turn off/down i.Resolution. The "i" isn't that intelligent & makes some nasty over-sharpened halos in some spots. My advice, if you like the overall look of the jpeg, shoot raw+jpeg & process the raw using the jpeg as a guide. This isn't needed all the time. Only some scenes have this problem.
8/14/2020 I never played with the weird 4K burst modes. I just mucked with them today. They tend to hang up the camera. They don't seem to offer much over the regular drive modes. They take up two programmable buttons I can put to better use.
7/18/2019 Low light. No camera of this type is going to do well in natural light at last light (9 PM here.) This one is noticeably worse than my SX720HS. And that's bad.
6/29/2019 With an upgraded SD card, I tried the high speed video. The 240 fps VGA mode worked like a dream. To access it, you have to have the camera on [Cinema Camera]M mode. WARNING: Objects in camera fall 1/8th as fast as real life. :)
6/24/2019. With hundreds of pictures down, I really like the flip screen. I also like the auto bracket. I tend to keep it on 1/3 stop; 2/3 seems to be a bit wide. I've turned off the touch screen. Moving the focus position with the tip of my nose whenever I use the EVF is right out.
6/21/2019. Video playback seems to be twitchy on this model. Apparently some cameras, some times have trouble playing back some videos. Check your memory card specs. Even with a high end card, playback is chancy. Recording is fine. Playback on a PC is fine.

6/17/2019. The only serious negative about this camera is the slight increase in size and weight over my old SX720HS. It's about twice the volume. It has reasons for that, with the added features, particularly the tilt-screen and the EVF.

I really like high-end, 1/2.3"-sensor, long-zoom, point & shoot cameras. This one is pretty close to the limit. Much more and you have to go to 1" sensor designs, which hurts your zoom range. I currently have:
-Canon SX280HS--great camera, still has features no one else has, terrible for videos (I don't care), battery hog (I do care)
-Canon SX720HS--basically the SX280HS perfected. I wouldn't normally upgrade this soon, but for,
-Panasonic ZS70--this camera, which I got for very short money (thanks Amazon warehouse)

* I wasn't that interested in the flip-up screen, I don't do selfies or vlogs. Boy was I wrong. It allows you to snake the camera into positions that would otherwise require a contortionist.
* I was interested in the EVF. It's good in dim light, but I'm used to eyeballing pictures from an external screen. Still a plus, but less of one than I thought.
* I was interested in the powerful bracketing functions. Still interested, but I'll need a bit more study to make it work.

Generally, I shoot in P mode or M mode. Both modes work fine on this camera. The autofocus is better than on the two Canons. The focus modes take a little experimentation to find the one that works best for you, but they all seem to work. 'Standard' color balance is fine. I need to play with 'Natural' a bit to see which one I prefer. The attached photos were all taken on standard. All on a single sunny morning walk after a rainy night in Massachusetts.

First impression? This is a really good camera, even at the list price.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic LUMIX DC-ZS70S, 20.3 Megapixel, 4K Digital Camera, Touch Enabled 3-inch 180 Degree Flip-front Display, 30X LEICA DC VARIO-ELMAR Lens, WiFi (Silver)

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Auto (1st gen) - Hands-free Alexa in your car with your phone The Echo Auto is a great item for the car, it simply can't do what you want it to do in the long run. The problems I have had with it are:
1. Cannot change the name of the device. For some reason this is not possible. Even if you wanted to name it "Car" or "Kia" or something logical, you will be unable to do so.
2. Pandora is not your phone's Pandora. Even if you can play music from Pandora via this device, if your phone is modified (like ad blocking) it breaks it's ability to play songs. No easy way to access the radio stations you have pre-configured. Should you not specify a radio station, be prepared to have your genre to be Rap and Hip Hop.
3. Getting it to call or send SMS is frustrating. You have to wait for the beep, then fight over which entry you really wanted. The pre-beep routine is not fluid for this. Its ability to select from the contacts is also compromised.

Overall, it does what it says it does. However, it's implementation of music control and calls/SMS needs much work. Lastly, the case needs a point to be able to hook it on something. Put a leash on it. Connect it to something. When you leave the car you need something to hang it on, like a lanyard...at least in my case.

Good enough to keep. The most frustrating of the Echo devices...
text_fidelity_b: Echo Auto (1st gen) - Hands-free Alexa in your car with your phone

text_fidelity_a:
Polk Audio ES35 Sound Wall Mount Speakers, Black & Polk Audio ES15 Wall Mount Bookshelf Speaker, Black I'm very pleased with all aspects of this center speaker. The sound quality is excellent. This replaces an old KEF center speaker and the difference can be clearly heard. The Polk has a crisp, clean sound that clarifies and enhances dialog but not at the expense of a nice solid bass (although I also have a subwoofer in the setup).

Aesthetically it's a simple, clean design. Normally I don't pay much attention to the look of a speaker but in this case, since it's a center speaker, it's in my line of sight all the time. It's about as unobtrusive you can get with a center speaker without compromising sound quality and performance. Polk did an excellent job with the design.

I looked at the new version of this (the ES35) and, while there are some small incremental improvements, I didn't consider them to be worth the extra $100 it costs. Plus, this was on a price dip for the differential between the two was $150, making this the clear choice.

While I have been partial to KEF in the past for speakers, the performance of this Polk has really wow'd me. At present I'm using this center speaker with KEF left and right front speakers, and KEF for surround. I've been so impressed with the ES35 that I'll be changing to Polk for my L/R soon, and keep the KEF only for surround (5.1.2 setup).

An excellent center speaker that hits the mark on all counts. Five stars.
text_fidelity_b: Polk Audio ES35 Sound Wall Mount Speakers, Black & Polk Audio ES15 Wall Mount Bookshelf Speaker, Black

Easy set up: Couldn't have been easier unless they unpacked it for me. From opening the box to streaming from my iPod touch was a matter of moments. No problem connecting at all.

Small footprint: You can see the precise measurements in the product description, but what I really like about it is how sleek/narrow it is, meaning it can fit on just about anything--a narrow shelf, a mantle, a dresser with a lot of stuff on it. While this is less of a concern in my house, I can see this being a big plus for a student in a dorm or someone in a small apartment.

Good sound: sound is crisp and clear and volume can go up surprisingly high. Bass isn't bad at all for such a small design. It's a surprisingly full sound, much better to be honest than I had expected.

Sturdy feel: it feels like it has a good heft to it and the materials feel well constructed. I assume I'll be moving it around quite a bit (I plan on using it outdoors more than anything so I no longer have to throw my speakers into a window when I sit on our patio) so it's nice to know I won't have to tiptoe around shoddy construction

Strong wireless connection: Our house is pretty small (1600 sq feet) so my connection stays pretty much wherever I am on the bottom floor. It doesn't matter what room I'm in--the walls don't have an impact. And we have a wireless network that gives it no problem at all.

Expandability: I also got the sub-woofer which really pumped up the bass in crisp, clean, room-filling fashion. I don't have any additional speakers, but I am actually considering it which comes as a bit of a surprise for a secondary system--that's how much I like this

Cons
Not fully portable: it does have to be plugged in, so you won't be tossing in a backpack and taking it to the park with you.

and um, that's about it for the cons.

In terms of sound quality, price, ease of use, size factor, expandability, there's nothing bad to say about the device and a lot of good. I'm extremely pleased with it all around, get a lot of use out of it, and imagine it as being used even more once weather turns warm again round here.

Highly recommended
text_fidelity_b: Creative ZiiSound D3x Bluetooth Wireless Speaker

(Old Model) Seagate 1TB Desktop HDD Sata 6Gb/s 64MB Cache 3.5-Inch Internal Bare Drive (ST1000DM003) I had this drive and it lasted exactly 2 years from the manufacturing date on the case. No click, no warning, nothing. Just won't boot, won't format, won't do anything. I did manage to get the computer to recognize what the drive model is, using Seatools. So the CMOS is there, but the drive won't read or write any data. Seatools came up with the diagnostics that I have 3 bad LBAs. The drive has a warranty for 3 years in my case. But I got to thinking, that I get excited and send in my drive for a new one and next my identity goes missing. I cannot format or delete anything. If I destroy the drive, then the warranty is null. Seagate is not a good drive in my opinion.
Funny thing, I went and got a USB case that will accept any hard drive, ide....I put in an old hdd that I dropped on the carpet. It was absolutely dead--I thought. It was absolutely functional and all the data I thought I lost was there untouched. I am thinking about dropping this one on the carpet. But I found a place that I can use to get the parts and fix it myself--maybe with luck. If not, I will try the carpet idea.
text_fidelity_b: (Old Model) Seagate 1TB Desktop HDD Sata 6Gb/s 64MB Cache 3.5-Inch Internal Bare Drive (ST1000DM003)
